Alcohol Use (Biblical)
AL-kuh-hol YOOS
noun phrase (Christian ethics)
The biblical doctrine of the lawful use of alcoholic beverages. Scripture presents wine and strong drink as a good gift of God to be received with thanksgiving and used in moderation (Psalm 104:15; 1 Timothy 5:23), while sternly condemning drunkenness as sin (Ephesians 5:18; Proverbs 23:29-35). Distinguished from the modern teetotal-abstinence position (total prohibition) and the libertine-excess position.

Biblical Definition

The biblical doctrine of the lawful use of alcoholic beverages. Scripture presents wine and strong drink in a substantively-balanced way that the patriarchal-Reformed reader holds against both the teetotal-abstinence position (total prohibition) and the libertine-excess position. The positive: wine is a good gift of God given to gladden the heart of man (Psalm 104:15, wine that maketh glad the heart of man); wine is used in the Passover and the Lord's Supper (Matthew 26:27-29); the Lord Jesus turned water into wine at Cana (John 2:1-11, His first miracle) and was accused of being a winebibber (Matthew 11:19, though falsely as to excess); Paul counsels Timothy to use a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23); wine is a sign of covenant blessing and feast-joy throughout Scripture (Deuteronomy 14:26; Amos 9:14). The negative: drunkenness is sternly condemned as sin (Ephesians 5:18, be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit; Galatians 5:21, drunkenness among the works of the flesh that exclude from the kingdom; Proverbs 23:29-35, the vivid portrait of the drunkard's misery; 1 Corinthians 6:10, drunkards shall not inherit the kingdom). The biblical doctrine: alcohol is a good gift of God to be received with thanksgiving and used in moderation; drunkenness is sin. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical balance against the modern American-evangelical teetotal-abstinence position (which arose substantially from the nineteenth-century temperance movement and lacks biblical warrant for total prohibition) and against the libertine-excess position. The substantive concern for the weaker brother (Romans 14; 1 Corinthians 8) counsels charitable consideration of those for whom alcohol is a substantive temptation, but does not establish a universal abstinence requirement.

Webster 1828 Definition

Biblical doctrine of the lawful use of alcohol; Scripture presents wine as a good gift of God to be received with thanksgiving and used in moderation (Psalm 104:15; 1 Timothy 5:23) while sternly condemning drunkenness as sin (Ephesians 5:18); distinguished from teetotal-abstinence and libertine-excess positions.

ALCOHOL USE (BIBLICAL), n. phr. (Christian ethics) Scripture presents wine and strong drink in a balanced way. Positive: wine gladdens the heart of man (Psalm 104:15); used in Passover and Lord's Supper (Matthew 26:27-29); Christ's first miracle was turning water into wine (John 2:1-11); Paul counsels a little wine for Timothy's stomach (1 Timothy 5:23); sign of covenant feast-joy (Deuteronomy 14:26). Negative: drunkenness sternly condemned (Ephesians 5:18; Galatians 5:21; Proverbs 23:29-35; 1 Corinthians 6:10). Doctrine: alcohol a good gift to be received with thanksgiving and used in moderation; drunkenness is sin. Held against the teetotal-abstinence position (nineteenth-century temperance movement, no biblical warrant for total prohibition) and the libertine-excess position.

Key Scripture

Psalm 104:14-15 — "He causeth the grass to grow for the cattle, and herb for the service of man: that he may bring forth food out of the earth; And wine that maketh glad the heart of man, and oil to make his face to shine, and bread which strengtheneth man's heart."

1 Timothy 5:23 — "Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities."

Ephesians 5:18 — "And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit."

John 2:9-10 — "When the ruler of the feast had tasted the water that was made wine... the governor of the feast called the bridegroom, And saith unto him, Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine; and when men have well drunk, then that which is worse: but thou hast kept the good wine until now."

Modern Corruption

The teetotal-abstinence position (total prohibition of alcohol) lacks biblical warrant; the libertine-excess position ignores the stern biblical condemnation of drunkenness; the biblical doctrine is moderate use with thanksgiving and the prohibition of drunkenness.

expand to see more

The biblical doctrine of alcohol use is held against two opposing errors. The teetotal-abstinence position (total prohibition of all alcohol consumption) arose substantially from the nineteenth-century American temperance movement and lacks biblical warrant for total prohibition: Scripture presents wine as a good gift of God (Psalm 104:15), the Lord Jesus made and drank wine (John 2; Matthew 11:19), Paul counseled Timothy to use a little wine (1 Timothy 5:23), and the Lord's Supper uses wine. The total-prohibition position requires reading the biblical commendation of wine as either referring to grape juice (an implausible reading given the impossibility of preserving unfermented grape juice in the ancient world and the explicit references to the intoxicating effect, John 2:10) or as a concession to be transcended (which has no biblical warrant). The libertine-excess position ignores the stern biblical condemnation of drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18; Galatians 5:21; 1 Corinthians 6:10; Proverbs 23:29-35). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine: alcohol is a good gift of God to be received with thanksgiving and used in moderation; drunkenness is sin; the substantive concern for the weaker brother counsels charitable consideration but does not establish a universal abstinence requirement; the mature Christian man may enjoy wine, beer, and strong drink in moderation as a good gift, with substantive guard against drunkenness and substantive charity toward those for whom alcohol is a particular temptation.

Hebrew Roots

Wine as good gift (Psalm 104:15; John 2; 1 Timothy 5:23); drunkenness condemned (Ephesians 5:18; Galatians 5:21); held against teetotalism and libertinism.
